notes.meaning: Jonathan heard David speak to Saul with deep faith and courage, and his heart was instantly drawn to David. Their two souls were tied together in a pure, brotherly affection. Jonathan was the crown prince, yet he loved David as much as he loved his own life.

other.label: Popular modern teaching
other.view: Some popular modern writers suggest Jonathan and David had a romantic or sexual relationship, rather than a devoted friendship.

notes.meaning: King Saul brought David into his royal court on a permanent basis. David was no longer allowed to slip away to tend sheep for his father Jesse. God used this royal appointment to train David for his future work as a ruler.

Jonathan made a formal covenant with David to seal their bond of friendship. A covenant was a sacred, lifelong promise made before God. They pledged to support each other and look out for each other's families.

Jonathan took off his own royal robe, military coat, sword, bow, and belt, and gave them to David. In the ancient world, wearing royal garments was one of the highest honors a subject could receive. By dressing David in his own prince's attire, Jonathan willingly showed that he accepted God's plan for David to reach the throne.

David obeyed every command Saul gave him and had great success in every battle. Because David acted with such wisdom, Saul put him in command of the fighting men. Both the common people and the king's royal officers were glad to see David honored.

As the Israelite soldiers returned from war, women came out from the towns to celebrate with songs, dances, and musical instruments. The women sang back and forth to each other in praise of the victory. But their song praised David for killing tens of thousands, while giving Saul credit for only thousands.

The song made Saul burn with anger because the higher praise was given to his servant instead of himself. Remembering that God had warned him about losing his crown, Saul immediately suspected David would take his throne. Saul's pride made him view another person's success as his own loss.

From that moment on, Saul watched David with bitter jealousy and suspicion. He looked for any sign that the young warrior might be disloyal. Envy completely changed how the king treated his most faithful servant.

The very next day, God permitted a distressing spirit to come over Saul, throwing him into an uncontrolled frenzy. David came to play the harp for him as he had done before, seeking to calm the troubled king. While David held an instrument of peace, Saul held a deadly war spear.

Saul hurled the spear straight at David, aiming to pin him to the wall. David saw the danger, dodged the strike, and escaped with his life twice. Instead of striking back at the king, David chose to leave his protection entirely in God's hands.

Saul grew deeply afraid of David because he could see that the Lord was with him. At the same time, the king knew the Lord had departed from his own life. Spiritual authority had clearly shifted from Saul to the young warrior.

Saul removed David from the royal palace and made him an officer over a thousand soldiers in the field. The king hoped to keep David away from court and expose him to constant danger on the battlefield. Instead, this gave David the chance to lead the troops directly and earn their deep respect.

David behaved with great wisdom and succeeded in all his duties because the Lord was with him. Even under unfair treatment and open danger, he never lost his self-control. God's presence guided his steps and blessed his efforts.

When Saul saw how wisely and successfully David managed every task, his dread of him only deepened. He realized he was dealing with a man whose good character and divine blessing could not be easily shaken. True godly wisdom often frightens those who are driven by malice.

The people of all Israel and Judah came to love David deeply. They saw him go out to battle and safely lead them home again. His humble service and brave leadership won the hearts of the entire nation.

Saul offered his oldest daughter Merab to David in marriage, urging him to fight bravely in the Lord's wars. This seemed like a generous reward, but Saul was secretly plotting David's death. He hoped the Philistines would kill David in battle so he would not have to murder him with his own hands.

David answered with genuine humility, asking who he or his family was to marry into the royal house. He had no selfish ambition and did not try to push his way to the throne. His humble spirit kept him from falling into Saul's schemes.

When the wedding day arrived, Saul broke his royal promise and gave Merab to a man named Adriel instead. This was a deliberate insult meant to provoke David into an angry or rebellious response. Breaking promises in this way showed how untrustworthy the king had become.

Saul learned that his younger daughter Michal was in love with David, and the news pleased him. He did not care about his daughter's happiness, but he welcomed a fresh opportunity to plot against David. Selfish rulers often treat their own family members as tools for their personal schemes.

Saul decided to use Michal as a trap to bring about David's death at the hands of the Philistines. He told David that he now had a second chance to become his son-in-law. Beneath his sweet-sounding words, the king hid a murderous plot.

Saul commanded his servants to speak with David in private and flatter him. They told David that the king delighted in him and that all the royal staff loved him. Saul did this behind the scenes so the marriage would look like the court's idea rather than his own trap.

David told the servants that becoming the king's son-in-law was a serious matter, especially for a poor man of low standing. In ancient Israel, a groom was expected to give a valuable bride-price to the bride's father. David knew he lacked the wealth and status needed to pay for a royal princess.

When Saul heard David's answer, he sent word that he wanted no money at all, but only the foreskins of one hundred Philistines. Saul disguised this as holy revenge against Israel's uncircumcised enemies. In reality, he set this extreme challenge hoping the Philistines would overwhelm and kill David.

David was glad for the chance to become the king's son-in-law, so he and his men went out before the time limit ended. They struck down two hundred Philistines and brought double the requested proof directly to Saul. Saul was forced to keep his word, and he gave his daughter Michal to David in marriage.

Saul was forced to see that the Lord was actively protecting David, and he also saw that his daughter Michal truly loved him. Instead of turning to God in repentance, Saul's fear deepened into continuous hatred. From that time on, the king treated David as an open, lifelong enemy.

Whenever the Philistine commanders marched out to battle, David fought with more skill and wisdom than any other officer under Saul. His victories made his name famous and deeply honored across the land. God continued to lift up David in public esteem even while the earthly king tried to destroy him.
